title: Motion Under a Time-Varying Force
short: Integrate F(t)/m to find the velocity when the force changes with time.
trouble: Students use the final force as if it had acted the whole time.

blocks.html: Newton's Second Law Along an Axis used forces that stay the same. Real pushes rarely do: a motor ramps up, a gust fades, a bat touches a ball for a few milliseconds. Newton's second law still holds at every instant, so the acceleration simply follows the force, and Velocity and Position from Acceleration does the rest.

With a net force $F(t)$ on a mass $m$: $$a(t) = \dfrac{F(t)}{m}, \qquad v(t) = v_0 + \dfrac{1}{m}\int_0^t F(t')\,dt'.$$ The change in velocity is the area under the force–time graph divided by the mass.

$F = ma$ is a statement about one instant: the net force now sets the acceleration now. Over a tiny time $dt$ the velocity changes by $dv = a\,dt = \dfrac{F}{m}\,dt$. Adding up all those small changes is an integral. The quantity $\int F\,dt$ is the impulse, which you'll meet again in Impulse as an Integral.

blocks.name: ph-graph

opts.task: Drag the right edge. The area (in N·s) divided by the mass is the speed gained.

blocks.cap: $F(t) = 6t$ on a 3 kg cart. The area from 0 to 4 s is $48\ \text{N·s}$, so the cart gains $48/3 = 16\ \text{m/s}$.

blocks.title: A force that grows
blocks.q: A $3\ \text{kg}$ cart starts from rest on a frictionless track, pushed by $F(t) = 6t$ (N, s). Find its speed and position at $t = 4\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: A push that fades out
blocks.q: A $5\ \text{kg}$ block on ice starts from rest. A push $F(t) = 40 - 10t$ (N, s) acts until it reaches zero. How fast is the block moving then?
steps: Geometrically, the area is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(40) = 80\ \text{N·s}$.

blocks.html: Using the final force as if it had acted the whole time. For the first cart, the force at 4 s is 24 N; $24 \times 4/3 = 32\ \text{m/s}$, twice the true 16 m/s, because the push was weaker early on. Using the starting force goes wrong the other way. Check: the answer must equal the area under the actual $F$–$t$ graph divided by $m$. A rectangle drawn at the final height is far bigger than the triangle under $F = 6t$.

If several forces act, add them first: $F_{\text{net}}(t) = F_{\text{push}}(t) - f_k$, and integrate the net force. The integral of one force alone gives only that force's share of the change in momentum.
